video_title: Sarah Paine — Why wars are so difficult to end
gist: Historian Sarah Paine delivers a lecture on why wars are hard to end, building a Clausewitz/Sun Tzu analytical framework (culminating point of attack vs. victory, limited vs. unlimited goals, 'land of death', denial-of-victory insurgency) from the Russo-Japanese War, Gulf War, Korean War, WWI, and Iraq, then explicitly applies that framework to assess why the Russia-Ukraine war persists and where its escalation risks lie.

themes.theme: Clausewitz/Sun Tzu framework for war endings

insights.claim: War outcomes should be judged by whether a side achieves its actual political goal, not by how many battles it won — the US won most conventional battles in Vietnam but the war is not counted as a victory, because it failed to achieve its underlying political objective.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Investors assessing an ongoing conflict (e.g., Ukraine) should track stated political objectives and their feasibility, not battlefield tallies, to judge how and when the war actually ends.
insights.quote: The United States won most of the conventional battles in the Vietnam War, and I don't think the war registers as a victory.

insights.claim: The single clearest signal that a belligerent has passed its 'culminating point of victory' (overextended relative to what is sustainable) is the intervention of a large third party, which changes the nature of the war.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Watch for signs of major third-party military or financial intervention in any live conflict as the trigger for reassessing escalation and duration risk.
insights.quote: One key indicator that you've passed the tipping point of victory is third-party intervention, which can change the, uh, nature of the war if the third party is large.

insights.claim: Wars are analytically either 'limited' (occupying territory to negotiate or annex) or 'unlimited' (regime change) goals; unlimited goals are conceptually simple but operationally brutal because the losing side has nothing left to lose and fights in what Sun Tzu called 'the land of death,' producing fanatical resistance.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: A regime-change objective should be priced as a much longer, costlier, higher-resistance scenario than a territorial/limited-goal conflict — relevant to modeling sanctions duration, defense spend, and commodity-supply disruption timelines.
insights.quote: The idea is that if you have an unlimited target, that means that at least the regime, uh, that is the victim of it is destined for destruction... And people in such a situation tend to fight to the death.

insights.claim: Whether an adversary collapses quickly under pressure ('shatters like a Bologna flask') or hardens its resolve after the first blow is genuinely unpredictable in advance and has to be judged case by case — Nicholas II's regime shattered after 1905, whereas other regimes have hardened under similar pressure.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Discounts confident forecasts that sanctions/military pressure will quickly force capitulation — regime fragility is not reliably predictable from outside, which should widen the range of scenarios investors hedge for.
insights.quote: The question is whether the first blow of the battle will steal the enemy's resolve and strengthen his resistance... or, like a jar of bologna, it will shatter as soon as its surface cracks.

themes.theme: Fiscal exhaustion as a war-ending mechanism (Russo-Japanese War)

insights.claim: In the Russo-Japanese War, Japan's borrowing costs fell as it won battles, letting it secure its final two war loans even after heavy losses, while Russia's credit dried up entirely after its defeat at Mukden and it could not find lenders for the war.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: War financing capacity (access to credit markets, cost of debt) can be as decisive as battlefield performance in ending a conflict — a lens for assessing which side in a modern conflict (e.g., Russia under sanctions) can sustain financing longest.
insights.quote: Russia went bankrupt... after the Battle of Mukden, when Russia desperately needed another loan, no one would take it and pay for it, because they did not consider Russia to be in a favorable position.

insights.claim: Money diverted to a war is an opportunity cost against other uses; Russia's spending on the Russo-Japanese War came at the expense of expanding its European rail network, an investment that would have materially helped it in World War I less than a decade later.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: War spending has multi-decade opportunity costs on unrelated infrastructure/capital investment — a reminder to model the long-tail fiscal drag of prolonged conflicts on a state's future capacity, not just current-year spend.
insights.quote: If Russia is spending money on this war, it means that it is not spending all that money on, say, something useful, which would be the expansion of its railway system in the European part of Russia. This would have been very useful in World War I.

insights.claim: Japan pre-planned its exit strategy before the war's decisive battles even occurred, cultivating Harvard-alumnus connections to Theodore Roosevelt years in advance specifically to secure US mediation once its army was exhausted.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Illustrates that successful war-termination requires lining up a third-party mediator/exit channel before military capacity runs out, not after — a template for reading whether a modern belligerent has a credible negotiated off-ramp prepared.
insights.quote: The exit strategy... will be President Theodore Roosevelt, who they are going to use to mediate the end of the war. They are counting on the Americans to intervene. Yes, and they calculated correctly.

themes.theme: Escalation pathology: regional wars becoming global

insights.claim: The American Revolution shows how fast a regional war can globalize: France allied with the American colonies in 1778, Spain allied with France in 1779, and Britain was fighting the Dutch by 1780, turning a colonial rebellion into a multi-theater global war within about three years.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: A conflict's duration and cost profile can shift discontinuously once it drags on long enough for rivals of the stronger power to see an opening to pile on — a timeline pattern (roughly 2-3 years) worth watching in current regional conflicts.
insights.quote: French ally with the colonies in 1778, then Spanish ally with the French in 1779, and...Britain attacks the Dutch in 1780. So, what was a regional war is turning into a global one.

insights.claim: World War I could not be settled through negotiation partly because each member of each alliance system wanted incompatible things (Britain wanted the status quo, France wanted Alsace-Lorraine back, Russia wanted Austria-Hungary out of the Balkans, Germany wanted colonies), so no coalition could agree on terms even among its own allies, let alone force capitulation on the other side.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Multilateral coalitions with divergent objectives structurally prolong wars because settlement requires unanimous agreement inside each bloc — relevant to reading NATO/EU cohesion as a variable in how quickly the Ukraine war can be negotiated to a close.
insights.quote: This means that even within the framework of alliance systems, the goals in this war do not coincide... And so, you get these parallel wars for different places.

insights.claim: The 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff, passed by the US to protect domestic jobs, triggered foreign retaliation that deepened the Great Depression globally; the resulting economic desperation in Japan (a founding League of Nations member that depended on trade) directly motivated its pivot to invading Manchuria to pursue economic autarky, which snowballed into the invasion of all China and eventually the Pacific War.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: A direct historical causal chain from unilateral protectionist tariffs to global depression to militarized autarky and world war — a cautionary precedent for pricing the geopolitical tail risk of aggressive modern tariff escalation.
insights.quote: They passed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, which raised U.S. tariffs skyrocketed... They strike with vengeance, tanks are traded around the world... This deepens the Great Depression.

insights.claim: Defeating a conventional army without securing the enemy's surrender invites a 'denial of victory' rebellion that is extremely expensive for the occupier to suppress indefinitely and even more costly for the insurgents fighting under harsh conditions — a dynamic Japan faced in China and the US faced in Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Occupying/stabilizing a country after a swift military win is often costlier than the initial war itself — a key variable in estimating the multi-decade fiscal and troop-commitment burden of any future regime-change intervention.
insights.quote: if you defeat someone conditionally, but they don't surrender, they start a rebellion against you, and this is a strategy of denial of victory. Incredibly expensive for someone who is denied victory because they are always there.

insights.claim: The 'value of the object' framework predicts that a home population defending its own territory values the outcome far more existentially than an outside intervening power does, and the further a power projects force from home, the lower its relative valuation of the objective — favoring the local defender/insurgent in a war of attrition.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Explains why locally-defended conflicts (e.g., Ukraine, past US counterinsurgencies) tend to outlast the expectations of the stronger outside power — a reason to discount forecasts that superior military/economic power alone will force a quick end.
insights.quote: Washington is counting on the fact that the American value of the object is higher than the British one, and this is usually true. If you live in a theater of war, this is your home. It's existential.

themes.theme: Gulf War I as the low-cost-war benchmark

insights.claim: The 1991 Gulf War succeeded at unusually low cost to the US because President Bush Sr. defined a clear, limited political objective in advance (National Security Directive 54: expel Iraq from Kuwait, restore the Kuwaiti government), rather than leaving the war's goal ambiguous the way the US did in Korea.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: A precisely-scoped, publicly stated political objective set before military action starts is a leading indicator of a conflict resolving quickly and cheaply; ambiguity in stated war aims (as in Korea) predicts a costlier, longer conflict.
insights.quote: in this war, Bush Sr. made it clear. There is National Security Directive 54, he laid it out.

insights.claim: In the Gulf War, coalition partners paid the US over $50 billion plus an additional $14 billion to other coalition partners to cover the cost of American troops, while total coalition deaths were only 392 (258 American) against Iraqi military deaths of 20,000-35,000 — an unusually low-cost, mostly externally financed war for the intervening power.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Shows the financing template for a 'good' war from a great power's perspective: broad diplomatic isolation of the target plus allied burden-sharing to externalize costs — a benchmark against which to judge how costly (and unfunded) current conflicts are by comparison.
insights.quote: They paid the United States over 50 billion dollars to pay for all the American troops and other things. Plus, they pay an additional 14 billion to various coalition partners.

insights.claim: Diplomatic isolation of the aggressor — nearly all rich countries plus almost all of Iraq's neighbors joining the coalition against it, echoing Russia's isolation in the Russo-Japanese War versus Japan's British alliance — is presented as a precondition for a cheap, decisive outcome for the intervening side.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: A useful screen for conflict outcomes: count how diplomatically isolated the aggressor is (versus how many great-power backers it retains) as a proxy for whether the war will be short and cheap or long and costly for whoever opposes it.
insights.quote: All the rich countries of the world, plus almost all their neighbors, are rising up against them. So, here's the problem. In a situation where you face a huge coalition, it just won't go well for you.

themes.theme: Korea and Iraq: the cost of ambiguous or overreaching goals

insights.claim: The Korean War became far more costly than it needed to be because the US never settled whether its goal was restoring the pre-war border (limited) or unifying the peninsula (unlimited); this hesitation, combined with China's ~1,400km unsealable land border with North Korea supplying an uninterrupted ally, dragged the war on and led to a permanent, still-ongoing US troop commitment on the peninsula.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: An indefinite, decades-long garrison commitment (as in Korea) is the realistic downside cost of failing to define a war's limited objective clearly at the outset — relevant to estimating the long-run fiscal tail of any current military commitment left similarly undefined.
insights.quote: the United States couldn't decide, 'Do we just want half the peninsula... Or, if we are on the rise militarily, perhaps we should take over the entire peninsula, an unlimited goal?' And this hesitation was truly costly.

insights.claim: Stabilizing post-2003 Iraq was structurally far harder than the 1991 Gulf War because the border to be secured expanded from 158 miles (Kuwait) to over 2,000 miles (all of Iraq), bringing in three neighbors with their own regional ambitions — Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Turkey — who inevitably became involved.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Border length and the number/ambition of neighboring powers is a concrete, quantifiable predictor of post-war stabilization cost — a screening variable for assessing intervention risk in any territory with multiple ambitious neighbors.
insights.quote: in the Kuwait War, in Gulf War 1, you're only dealing with 158 miles of that border. In taking over this whole place, you're dealing with over 2,000 miles of this border.

insights.claim: Nation-building fails in 'mosaic societies' like Iraq where primary identity is ethnic/sectarian rather than national, because building shared state institutions is nearly impossible when factions are focused on eliminating rival identity groups rather than cooperating — unlike Korea, where all sides share an undisputed national identity and the fight is purely over which institutions govern it.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Whether a target country has a mosaic (multi-ethnic/sectarian) or unified national identity is a knowable-in-advance predictor of whether post-regime-change stabilization/reconstruction is even achievable — a due-diligence variable for reconstruction-linked investment or aid commitments.
insights.quote: in Iraq, primary identities seem to be more related to ethnic identity than to national identity... In these mosaic societies, where you don't even have a national identity, you won't be able to build state institutions.

insights.claim: Russia holds an unlimited goal toward Ukraine (regime change) while Ukraine holds only a limited goal toward Russia, which the speaker cites as her framework's core lens for interpreting the current war's trajectory and Ukraine's continued resistance.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Under this framework, Russia's unlimited objective implies Ukraine has little incentive to negotiate short of existential threat (per the 'land of death' logic), predicting a longer, harder-to-settle war than a symmetric limited-goals conflict would produce.
insights.quote: Russia has an unlimited goal towards Ukraine, and Ukraine has a limited goal towards Russia.

insights.claim: The war in Ukraine is asymmetric in the 'value of the object': it is existential and far more important to Ukrainians, who are fighting on their own soil, than to Russians, despite Russia's heavier absolute losses — which the speaker uses to explain why Ukrainian resistance has defied outside expectations.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: This value-of-the-object asymmetry argues against forecasts of a quick Russian battlefield win forcing Ukrainian capitulation, and supports pricing in a protracted conflict/sanctions regime rather than a near-term resolution.
insights.quote: I bet that what is happening in Ukraine interests Ukrainians much more than Russians. Isn't that right? The Russians suffered really heavy losses, so it's interesting, but for the Ukrainians it would be even more interesting because this is where they live.

insights.claim: Because Russia is pursuing an unlimited (regime-change) goal against Ukraine, it has effectively pushed Ukrainians into Sun Tzu's 'land of death,' where they fight with unusual desperation and resilience precisely because there is no survivable alternative to resisting.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: This mechanism suggests that further escalation of Russian aims (rather than de-escalation) is likely to harden rather than break Ukrainian resistance, a consideration for modeling how sanctions/negotiation leverage actually shifts Kremlin incentives.
insights.quote: The Russians sent them to the land of death, and the Ukrainians don't give up, uh, if they can avoid it, because they are dead people, many of them.

insights.claim: The speaker frames the risk that the regional Russia-Ukraine war escalates into a global war (via large third-party intervention, echoing WWI and the American Revolution) as the central pathology to monitor, alongside whether either side's culminating point of attack or victory has already been passed or not yet reached.
insights.speaker: Sarah Paine (guest, historian)
insights.so_what: Positions large-power direct intervention (NATO or otherwise) as the key tail-risk trigger that would reprice the conflict from a regional/contained event to a global-war scenario with far larger market implications.
insights.quote: This is the big fear about Ukrainian-Russian relations today: it's a surge, and suddenly it turns into a global war.
